tip: The ‘-an’ ending builds a describing clause: ‘mısır satan amca’ = the uncle who sells corn. ‘satan’ describes ‘amca’.
Possession pairs two endings: the owner gets ‘-ın’, the thing gets ‘-sı’, giving ‘babamın arabası’ = my father's car.
Proper names take an apostrophe before a case ending: ‘Ankara'da’ = in Ankara. Common nouns skip it, like ‘hastanede’.
The ‘-diği/-tiği’ ending builds a past describing clause on an object: ‘kaybettiği anahtar’ = the key that he lost.
The ‘-ce’ ending turns an adjective into a manner adverb: ‘sessizce’ = quietly, from ‘sessiz’ = quiet.
‘henüz’ means 'yet'. With a negative verb like ‘gelmedi’ it means 'not yet': ‘onlar henüz gelmedi’ = they haven't come yet.
The suffix ‘-dan/-den’ marks the source, 'from': ‘arkadaşımdan’ = from my friend.
Add ‘-la/-le’ to a noun to make a manner adverb: ‘mutluluk’ (happiness) plus ‘-la’ gives ‘mutlulukla’ = happily.
Verb stem plus ‘-maya/-meye’ shows purpose, 'in order to': ‘almaya’ = to buy, telling why you ‘gittim’ (went).
‘yanında’ means 'next to'; the noun before it takes the owner ending ‘-ın’: ‘fırının yanında’ = next to the bakery.
The suffix ‘-acak/-ecek’ makes the future tense: ‘yat-’ (go to bed) plus ‘-acağım’ gives ‘yatacağım’ = I will go to bed.
‘yakın’ (near) needs the 'to' ending ‘-a/-e’ on what you are near: ‘denize yakın’ = close to the sea.
‘etmek’ turns a noun into a verb: ‘ziyaret’ (a visit) plus ‘ettik’ gives ‘ziyaret ettik’ = we visited.
‘mı’ is the yes/no question word; it stays separate and sits after the thing asked about: ‘araban mı’ = is it your car.
The suffix ‘-malı/-meli’ means 'must/should': ‘olmalıyız’ = we should be, ‘söylememeliyiz’ = we shouldn't say.
In a noun-plus-noun compound the second noun takes ‘-i’: ‘tatil’ (holiday) plus ‘ev’ gives ‘tatil evi’ = holiday house.
Put ‘en’ before an adjective to mean 'most': ‘en güzel’ = the most beautiful.
Add ‘-ki’ after a place ending to mean 'the one at/in': ‘vitrinindeki’ = the one in the shop window.
The suffix ‘-li/-lı’ means 'having': ‘güneş’ (sun) plus ‘-li’ gives ‘güneşli’ = sunny.
The ‘-sın’ ending gives a let-him/her command: ‘oynasın’ = let him play.
After a number, ‘-lik’ means 'consisting of / sized for': ‘beş kişilik’ = of five people (five-person).
Possession links two suffixes: the owner takes ‘-ın’, the thing takes ‘-ı’: ‘halasının evi’ = his aunt's house.
‘ayrılmak’ (to leave) takes the 'from' ending ‘-den’ on the place: ‘hastaneden ayrıldı’ = left the hospital.
The suffix ‘-mış’ reports something inferred from evidence, not witnessed: ‘ıslanmış’ = they have gotten wet (I see the result).
Verb stem plus ‘-ınca/-ince’ means 'when/upon doing': ‘bakınca’ = when you look.
‘-mış’ on your own action marks a sudden realization: ‘unutmuşum’ = oh, I've forgotten (I just noticed).
The habit ending ‘-ar/-er’ states habits and general truths: ‘kalkar’ = gets up, ‘bakar’ = tends, done regularly.
The negative ending ‘-emez/-amaz’ means 'cannot' and often 'not allowed': ‘içemezsiniz’ = you can't smoke.
For comparisons use ‘daha’ (more) and mark the thing compared with ‘-dan’: ‘Ankara'dan daha kalabalık’ = more crowded than Ankara.
Infinitive plus ‘için’ means 'in order to': ‘önlemek için’ = in order to prevent.
